faq.a: Yes, core elements such as early mobilisation and multimodal analgesia are still beneficial, though pre‑op optimisation may be limited.
faq.q: Can ERAS be used for emergency surgery?

faq.a: Give clear fluids (water or tea) up to 2 h before surgery and resume oral intake as soon as tolerated post‑op.
faq.q: What if a patient cannot tolerate oral carbohydrate drinks?

faq.a: Use clinical markers: blood pressure, heart rate, urine output ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h, and capillary refill.
faq.q: How to monitor fluid therapy without advanced cardiac output devices?

exam: What pre‑operative measure in ERAS reduces insulin resistance and why? — Carbohydrate loading; it maintains glycogen stores and blunts the stress‑induced hyperglycaemia.

A patient develops tachycardia and low urine output on day 2 post‑colorectal resection. Which ERAS component should you reassess first? — Fluid management; inadequate goal‑directed therapy may cause hypovolaemia.
Why are routine nasogastric tubes discouraged in ERAS pathways? — They increase pulmonary complications and delay return of gut function.

In a low‑resource hospital lacking epidural kits, how would you achieve multimodal analgesia for abdominal surgery? — Combine regular paracetamol, NSAID (if renal function permits), and peripheral nerve block with local anaesthetic.

A patient with chronic kidney disease cannot receive NSAIDs. How does this affect the ERAS analgesic plan? — Substitute with acetaminophen and consider low‑dose opioid or regional technique; avoid NSAID‑related nephrotoxicity.
Explain how early mobilisation reduces postoperative pulmonary complications. — Mobilisation improves ventilation‑perfusion matching, promotes cough, and prevents atelectasis.

During intra‑operative blood loss estimation, you lack a calibrated suction canister. What clinical signs guide fluid replacement? — Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, urine output, and surgical field appearance.
What is the most important reason to avoid prolonged fasting before surgery in ERAS? — Prolonged fasting increases insulin resistance and dehydration, worsening postoperative recovery.
ai.title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: ERAS is a multimodal, evidence‑based pathway that reduces surgical stress, speeds recovery, and lowers complications. It integrates pre‑operative counseling, optimized anesthesia, minimal invasive techniques, and early mobilisation.

b: Multidisciplinary team: surgeon, anaesthetist, nurse, physiotherapist, dietitian
Goal: reduce length of stay without increasing morbidity
sections.p: ERAS combines pre‑operative, intra‑operative and post‑operative interventions to attenuate the physiological stress response and promote early return of function.

b: Pre‑op: patient education, nutrition optimisation, carbohydrate loading
Intra‑op: minimally invasive technique, goal‑directed fluid therapy, multimodal analgesia
Post‑op: early oral intake, mobilisation within 6 h, avoidance of tubes/drains when possible
sections.p: Core elements are standardised across the peri‑operative period and should be applied to all eligible patients, especially in low‑resource settings where complications are costly.

b: Reduces postoperative pulmonary complications – crucial where ventilators are scarce
Lowers surgical site infection risk by limiting catheter use
sections.p: In East African hospitals, ERAS can offset limited ICU capacity and high infection rates by shortening hospital stay and reducing wound complications.
Investigations support safe progression through the pathway; when unavailable, clinical judgement replaces them.

t.b: Is the patient anaemic? – If <12 g/dL (women) or <13 g/dL (men) consider iron optimisation; if unavailable, assess pallor and fatigue
Detect dehydration or electrolyte imbalance before surgery – if not possible, check for orthostatic hypotension and dry mucous membranes
Guides fluid replacement – if quantitative measurement unavailable, use visual assessment and urine output

b: Carbohydrate drink 2 h before surgery – reduces insulin resistance; if drinks unavailable, give clear fluids up to 2 h pre‑op
Goal‑directed fluid therapy – use crystalloids to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg; avoid liberal fluids that cause oedema
Multimodal analgesia – paracetamol + NSAID (if no renal contraindication) + regional block; avoid high‑dose opioids to prevent respiratory depression
Early mobilisation – sit up within 6 h, ambulate next day; if physiotherapy staff limited, train nursing staff to assist
sections.p: Apply the ERAS bundle step‑by‑step; adapt each element to local resources.

b: Explain the physiological basis of pre‑op carbohydrate loading
Describe how goal‑directed fluid therapy reduces anastomotic leak risk
Identify which analgesic combinations are contraindicated in renal failure
sections.p: Examiners test understanding of why each ERAS component matters and how to modify it when resources are limited.

b: Skipping pre‑op nutrition assessment – leads to delayed wound healing
Routine use of nasogastric tubes – increases pulmonary complications
Over‑reliance on opioids – prolongs ileus and sedation
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from incomplete implementation or inappropriate deviation from the protocol.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe postoperative pain unresponsive to multimodal regimen
Signs of anastomotic leak: fever, tachycardia, abdominal tenderness
